title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Gdansk
paragraphs: I recently studied abroad at the Medical University of Gdansk in Poland. Gdansk is a somewhat minor city, so I will begin by introducing the city.

Gdansk is a port town in Poland on the Baltic Sea, belonging to the region once called the Polish Corridor. On the outskirts there is a headland called Westerplatte, which was the first place attacked when the German army began its invasion of Poland in the Second World War. After the war, the German residents were expelled by the Red Army, and it became a major shipyard of the Eastern bloc. The Gdansk shipyard also left its name in world history as the place where Lech Walesa (former president) formed "Solidarity" as part of the Polish democratization movement. Poland has such a tragic past, sandwiched between the great powers of Germany to the west and Russia to the east, and I was struck that locally, feelings toward Russia were worse than feelings toward Germany.

In this Gdansk, for about three months from March 18 to June 10, 2012, I rotated through the biochemistry department (Professor Wozniak), trauma surgery and obstetrics. The Medical University of Gdansk has an English course, with students from Sweden, the United Kingdom and Germany enrolled, and 40% of the total were international students. In addition, the students are basically bilingual or trilingual, so they communicated in English at the university and hospital.

I would like to look back on my life abroad by taking a day in trauma surgery as an example. In the morning there is a conference at 7:30, but it is in Polish. Sometimes a young doctor explained to me what the current patient meant. When I was there, they had just moved to the new ward and there were quite few inpatients. Rounds started around 9, and in the afternoon I observed surgery. My impression was that it was not much different from Polyclinic 1 in Japan. If I had time left in the evening, I went to Dr. Wozniak's department.

There are interesting points in the Polish healthcare system. In this country there is basically universal health insurance. However, it is also true that an outdated system remains even now, 20 years after the democratic revolution. Under the current insurance system, at the beginning of the year the number of occurrences of all kinds of diseases and the number of operations are forecast, and the budget is distributed on that basis. It often happens that the budget is exceeded by the end of the year, and when the money allocated at the beginning of the year runs out, the patient pays the full amount. So in December, when the national budget runs out, patients avoid going to hospitals, and the hospitals are said to be deserted. Naturally, the students' clerkships also seem to be easy (?) in this period. Aspects of a planned economy still remain, and local doctors and students lamented it. Also, once one becomes a doctor, one can work anywhere within the EU, so many doctors are said to want to go to Western countries in search of better pay. In particular, since there are many Polish immigrants in the United Kingdom and they have their own communities, some people reportedly use low-cost carriers to go to the United Kingdom to work part-time for several days a week and work in Polish hospitals the rest of the time. Doctors from Ukraine and the Balkan countries further east also reportedly come to Poland in search of better working conditions. It is truly the middle of globalization, but taxpayers did not seem to accept doctors trained with their country's taxes working in other countries.

What impressed me most was faith and religion. In Poland there are many devout Catholics, and I too was often asked about the religion I believe in. Some people pressed further and asked with serious faces, "Do you believe in the existence of the soul?" or "What do you think about the world after death?" When I thought about how they are conscious of God and the soul even in their daily lives and when working in medical settings, I thought they were different from Japanese people.

Finally, I am grateful for having been given more valuable experiences than I had expected. I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 坂本, Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 伊藤 and Ms. 山崎 of the International Exchange Office, Mr. 西尾 of the Academic Affairs office, Dr. Wozniak, and the doctors of the Gdansk Society, who supported me. Thank you very much.
